extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of journalism/media studies; journalists and newsroom personnel
extracted.subtask_description: Observed standards and practical criteria for producing, editing, and selecting local television news stories—covering narrative form, visual framing, technical continuity, timing, and newsworthiness as shaped by newsroom organization and professional routines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conformity to the accepted narrative form
rubrics_metrics.description: Film or videotape should conform to an accepted narrative form (beginning/middle/end) rather than a poetic or idiosyncratic treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrative-form material facilitates work by editors and other staff, reduces decoding time, and lessens the risk that a crew’s conception will be transformed or rejected. Idiosyncratic or poetic footage requires extra decoding and editing time and may be criticized as 'could not be worked with.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid idiosyncratic/poetic treatments
rubrics_metrics.description: Footage that eschews narrative in favor of poetic or highly personal vision is difficult for others to decode and incorporate into newsroom workflows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sol Worth experiment: narrative films were easiest for viewers to recount; poetic treatments required decoding the author’s vision. Reporters should avoid idiosyncratic material when organizational constraints make re-editing unlikely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of standardized visual symbols/lexicon
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ standard shots and visual symbols (e.g., picketers outside an airport for opposition, talking head in front of microphones for legitimated officials, flooded houses to symbolize flood damage) that connote the 'web of facticity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such symbols, if shown long enough (at least ten seconds), can register claims about reality; they usually complement the soundtrack and help viewers immediately interpret events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide visual variation to sustain audience interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories should include visual variation (not merely talking heads) to maintain viewer attention and protect ratings and ad revenue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visual variation can be achieved within a single story (mix of sound/silent film, demonstrations, interviews) or across a program (pacing and placement of upbeat features). Too many similar visuals can reduce variation and lead editors to omit additional similar items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow standard basic and complex unit structures and durations
rubrics_metrics.description: Assemble stories from recognized basic units (Unit A: silent film; Unit B: sound film) and complex narratives built from these units; basic units typically last 15–45 seconds, complex narratives 1–8 minutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tabled combinations (e.g., introduction/Unit B/closing, introduction/Unit A/Unit B/closing) to construct predictable, editable packages that match newsroom timing and format expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adhere to format and script symbols for technical continuity
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide script-format notations (e.g., 'Color sound film... lasting two minutes fourteen seconds') that cue directors, engineers, and technicians about timing, required cues, and expected picture/sound behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The format tells the director what to expect on monitors and when to institute corrective procedures; correct notation reduces split-second errors during live broadcasts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accommodate extreme timing constraints (organizational urgency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Accept that stories may need to be cut and aired under tight time pressures (sometimes in minutes) to get them on air before they become obsolete ('mere history').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rapidly assembled stories may not meet all professional-technical standards but satisfy the crucial organizational concern of timeliness; crews should provide material that can be edited quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think visually—seek illustrative visuals for verbal claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters and cameraworkers should 'think visually,' seeking shots that illustrate or symbolize the audio content (e.g., shooting beads on a tree to illustrate a doctor's comment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thinking visually helps avoid boring talking-head pieces and provides editors with usable footage; crews are encouraged to look for opportunistic visuals even for minor details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Align audio and visuals where possible; be aware of potential contradictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Visuals should generally complement the soundtrack to present coherent claims; however, deliberate or accidental misalignment can produce different interpretations (e.g., Vietnam footage visuals vs. political voice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors/reporters must recognize the tension between political narration (voice) and pictorial reportage; mismatches can create unintended meanings such as feelings of senselessness or war-weariness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of cutaways to prevent audio-visual jump-cuts
rubrics_metrics.description: When splicing sound film, insert 24–26 frames of silent film (cutaways) between recorded statements to avoid synchronization jumps due to camera/sound-track frame offsets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical cutaways include faces of the reporter listening or sound film of the reporter asking a question filmed after the formal interview; this is a standard technical editing practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition that feature (soft) news permits poetic/experimental techniques but needs more editorial work
rubrics_metrics.description: Feature stories may break hard-news rules (shorter shot durations, special lighting/distortion, unconventional framing) to achieve a poetic effect, but they require more careful editing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Features can use lighting, distortion, silhouette, intimate distances, and nonstandard camera angles to produce cinematic effects; such techniques are tolerated for features but are generally avoided for hard news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use upbeat features and 'kickers' to provide program variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Place upbeat feature stories or 'kickers' near the program end to provide tonal variation and close the program on an engaging note.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because kickers are often last, they may be labelled as such even if not humorous; features sometimes aim for poetic rather than narrative vision and are edited differently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conformity facilitates organizational flexibility and reuse
rubrics_metrics.description: Footage that conforms to standard narrative and formal conventions is more easily reused, allows generalist crews to cover a variety of assignments, and supports rapid reassignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because local crews often act as generalists and may receive new assignments rapidly, they should avoid idiosyncratic filming that limits editors’ ability to repurpose footage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness: primacy of events over issues (event orientation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Newswork privileges concrete, temporally anchored events (who/what/when/where/why/how) over analytic or structural issues that lack discrete temporal markers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Issues like 'institutionalized racism' or consciousness-raising activities are harder to render as news because they lack clear beginnings/ends or single spokespeople; reporters' craft habits (present orientation, logic of the concrete) bias coverage toward events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Access and legitimacy shape coverage (anchor of news nets)
rubrics_metrics.description: News organizations and reporters are more accessible to recognized, legitimated sources (institutions, spokespersons); groups with established media contacts gain coverage more easily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resource-poor groups must recruit middle-class supporters, advocate journalists, or generate novel/timely spectacles to penetrate news nets; public relations tactics (e.g., novel settings) can shift coverage into soft news if they emphasize novelty over timeliness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on 'firsts' and recognized spokespeople for story framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters often seek 'first' examples or single recognizable spokespersons to anchor a story; absence of elected/recognized spokespeople (as in many consciousness-raising groups) makes coverage difficult.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interviewing a 'first' tends to produce moderate/exceptional viewpoints and can depoliticize broader social issues; movements lacking representativeness or single voices are less likely to be framed as newsworthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framing through juxtaposition (narrative linkage)
rubrics_metrics.description: By juxtaposing visuals of related actors (e.g., council members and demonstrators), stories can frame separate occurrences as interconnected, thereby negating idiosyncrasy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and reporters can force different groups or events into the same context through formal concerns about visual variation and program pacing, effectively framing them as part of a common narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational rewards and sanctions shape reporting behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors control assignments and can reward or punish reporters (e.g., assigning 'good' stories to favored reporters or omitting optional on-camera shots that earn reporters extra fees) based on conformity to newsroom expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters who produce footage deemed 'not workable' risk status loss and reduced income; awareness of these organizational incentives influences how reporters shoot and package stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of standardized timing and director's clock for split-second coordination
rubrics_metrics.description: Directors rely on split-second timing divisions and standard cues in the format to coordinate multiple personnel (assistant director, engineers, technical operators, studio floor) during broadcast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear indications of whether split-second timing is mandatory or optional allow the director to give accurate orders; deviations (e.g., silent film when sound expected) prompt immediate corrective actions.
